title: The Five Key Fears?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. flips his five key beliefs of student motivation (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy) into their dark counterparts, five fears students may carry. Opening with Edward Hallowell's claim that fear is the most dangerous disability, he spells out what each anti-belief sounds like in a student's head. He argues that many educational problems trace back to these fears, which justifies studying and building systems around the beliefs. He then points to his Moments of Genuine Connection strategy as an efficient way to build credibility and belonging, which in turn lift the other three beliefs. Citing Hallowell again, he suggests that reducing fear frees up the brainpower students would otherwise spend on self-protection. The post closes by asking for other simple methods and plugs his motivation course.
points: Each of the five motivation beliefs has an opposite fear, such as feeling an outsider or thinking effort will not help, and naming them makes the stakes concrete.
The author claims that many problems in education come back to these five fears rather than to students' lack of ability.
Credibility and belonging are the leverage points, because building them makes value, effort and efficacy easier to build.
Fear consumes mental capacity, so a supportive classroom frees brainpower for learning content.
Small, student-by-student connection efforts are presented as a simple, high-yield practice for teachers.
quotes: As a specialist in learning disabilities, I have found that the most dangerous disability is not any formally diagnosable condition like dyslexia or ADD. It is fear.
These are fears. And even as I write their descriptors, I feel their weight. I see the student faces who voice things like this.
They remind me of the meaning of the word “oppressive” — a thing that keeps on in “subservience and hardship.” So many of the problems we see in education come back to these five key fears.

And that’s part of why the five key beliefs matter so much. It’s why we’re smart to give them our time and attention — to study them, experiment with them, work at them with our colleagues, build systems and policies that support them in our communities.

Just consider the preposterously simple “Moments of Genuine Connection” strategy I’ve written about so often. This is the student-by-student, hyper-efficient approach to building credibility (remember, one part of the CCP of credibility is Care) and belonging. From these two beliefs, you’ve got way more leverage at building value, effort, and efficacy.

Edward Hallowell, a psychiatrist with decades of cases in his history and author of the Harvard Business Review collection from which this post gets its epigraph, writes that “fostering connections and reducing fear promote brainpower.” Is it any wonder? When our students learn in environments supportive of the five key beliefs, the immense brainpower previously required for self-protection in a fearful environment becomes accessible for the work of mastering physics or learning about human health.
